AJK.name: Juneau
AJK.excerpt: /Saturday through Tuesday/... Long range forecast remains on track; Sunday remains a favorable day, with lighter winds and perhaps seeing a bit of low angle sun action. Will have to monitor fog potential over Sunday, stay tuned.

sections.name: Synopsis
paragraphs: - Multiple rounds of rain and wind are expected through the end of the week with increasing possibility of some drier and cooler weather this weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: /Through Friday night/ More fronts moving from SE to NW through the panhandle continue to be the main drivers of the forecast today. The first of these fronts is as of 4 am weakening over Admiralty and Baranof Islands, while a second frontal band is moving over Prince of Wales Island and Misty Fjords area. Neither of these features has any really significant winds with it though the first front is causing some N winds of 15 to 25 kt through the northern inner channels this morning. Radar and satellite imagery is also showing that the first front is shearing apart over the central panhandle currently.

These frontal features are expected to gradually weaken through the day and eventually merge with the trough that has the remains of a low currently W of Haida Gwaii. That overall trough will move N through the panhandle Thursday evening and into Canada Friday. Behind it westerly onshore flow will become dominate which will keep clouds with a chance of showers in the forecast into Friday night. Most of the effects of precip (mostly rain, though far northern areas could see some mix of rain and snow Thursday morning) and wind (highest around 25 kt in some northern channels Thursday morning) from these features will mainly be S and E of Cape Fairweather. Inner channel winds will also showcase a switch in wind direction from Northerly to southerly Thursday night into Friday as the trough moves into Canada and ridging builds into the southern panhandle behind it. Overall trend in the forecast is toward slightly drier, and somewhat warmer conditions into the start of the weekend.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: /Saturday through Tuesday/... Long range forecast remains on track; Sunday remains a favorable day, with lighter winds and perhaps seeing a bit of low angle sun action. Will have to monitor fog potential over Sunday, stay tuned. Outflow winds build Sunday night. Primary forecast challenge Wednesday night is diagnosing a shortwave trough moving through the gulf Saturday, shearing apart as it hits the coast bringing in some precipitation. As of Wednesday night, our forecast for Saturday shows no snow accumulation for communities along the Icy Strait Corridor with the snow level likely near 1000ft to 2000ft (for Icy Strait to Taku). For Haines and Skagway primary impact will be on upper elevation passes, with the limiting factor for Haines the southwesterly flow coming across the Chilkat Range. For White Pass will have to watch how far north higher moisture can sneak in. Current forecast has an inch or two heading up the hill near the pass Friday into Saturday. Current guidance has higher moisture in the central Panhandle, if this can sneak north a bit it would bring a few more inches of snow. Stay tuned.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: An active and unsettled pattern will continue through next week, with moist southwest flow continuing valley rain and mountain snow through Tuesday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Valley rain and mountain snow moving in from the northwest this afternoon, with warm temperatures raising snow levels to 6500-7500 feet.
- Gusty winds in southern areas and brief heavy rain with cold frontal passage Friday night into Saturday morning.
- Valley fog with dry and warm conditions expected late Saturday into Sunday, with unsettled cooler and wetter weather returning early next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Zonal flow aloft and a strong atmospheric river is bringing significant moisture to the northwest (over 6 inches of rain in the Olympic Peninsula in the last 24 hours!) this morning, with increasing cloud cover over southeast Oregon and southwest Idaho. Warm temperatures with breezy southeast winds will continue through the early morning, with a line of precipitation moving from the northwest into southeast Oregon by early Thursday afternoon. Temperatures remain warmer than forecast thanks to breezy southerly winds, so the low threat of freezing rain is isolated to sheltered valleys on Highway 26 in southern Baker County and Highway 20 in northern Malheur County. Snow levels will stay around 5000-6000 feet initially MSL, rising to 7000-8000 feet MSL by the evening. Areas in northern Adams/Valley county will see snow levels stay slightly lower around 5500-6500 feet MSL thanks to the strong mid level jet staying over southern Oregon/Idaho. This will lead to some further uncertainty on snow amounts in the Long Valley, especially on Highway 55 and 93. Snow amounts will likely only be between 1 and 3 inches, but there is a 10% chance of these higher elevation travel corridors seeing up to 5 inches of snow by Saturday morning. Rain and high mountain snow will continue for areas north of the Treasure Valley through Friday evening.

A robust cold front will then move through the region overnight on Friday with gusty winds of 40-50 mph southwest of the Snake Plain and heavy rain/snow showers. Precipitation will continue to expand south into the Lower Snake Plain through Saturday morning, with forecast confidence increasing in most mountain locations seeing at least an inch of liquid equivalent precipitation by Saturday afternoon. Precipitation amounts over the Treasure Valley from Thanksgiving Day through Saturday afternoon will be around 0.15-0.25 inches of total rainfall. Localized higher amounts are possible with any stronger showers that move through, especially along the cold front on Saturday. Snowfall totals today through Saturday afternoon will be around 4-8 inches above 7000 feet MSL, with much higher accumulations of up to 2 feet on mountain summits above 8000 feet MSL. As a ridge of high pressure builds back in and cold northwest flow exits to the east, dry and warm conditions will return briefly late Saturday and for most of the day on Sunday. A quick moving shortwave trough will move into the region late Sunday, bringing another round of precipitation over high terrain and a slight cool down.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: An active and unsettled pattern will continue through next week, with moist southwest flow continuing valley rain and mountain snow through Tuesday. A closed low will help split the upper level flow on Tuesday, bringing a deep upper level trough over the region and pushing much colder air into the region by Tuesday and Wednesday. This will lower snow levels to 4000-5000 feet MSL by Tuesday. The closed low and bulk of precipitation will likely stay to the south of our region on Wednesday, with the best chance of showers over the southern tier of our CWA near the Nevada border. As this low swings east, a quick building ridge of high pressure will bring warm and dry conditions late Wednesday into Thursday. Another weak shortwave trough will move over Washington State and northern Idaho by midweek, bringing another chance of light rain and mountain snow late Thursday into Friday. Uncertainty remains on the timing and exact location of these successive shortwave troughs, so precipitation chances remain around 15-40% on Wednesday and Thursday. Temperatures will remain around 4-8 degrees above normal through the long term period.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: This system will move off to the east late Saturday, leaving colder and drier conditions for Sunday. Lows Sunday morning in the plains will be in the teens to 20s and highs will be in the 40s.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Gusty winds expected along the northern Front Range and northern border area Friday, spreading to all the plains Saturday.
- Snow and blowing snow in the mountains for Thanksgiving weekend travel. Banded rain/snow showers possible for the plains and I-25 Corridor Saturday - Saturday night.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A chilly Thanksgiving morning with lows generally in the 20s across the plains will give way to above normal temperatures in the afternoon. Highs for Thanksgiving will be in the 50s to near 60 for the plains and 30s to mid 40s for the mountains and valleys. Winds will remain on the lighter side with mostly sunny to partly cloudy skies for the holiday.

For the system this weekend, the GFS has trended closer to what the Euro (and a few other models) has been showing over the past few days. The increased model consensus has allowed our forecast confidence to increase for this weekend. Upper level northwest flow will strengthen on Friday, bringing breezy conditions to the higher terrain starting Friday morning. Wind gusts will be around 40 to 65mph on Friday for elevations generally above 9000ft. We could see some stronger winds come off of the Cheyenne ridge and into our northern plains counties Friday afternoon as well, with gusts around 25 to 40mph. Downsloping northwest winds will allow temperatures to warm further, putting highs around 60 degrees for much of the plains on Friday.

An upper level shortwave will approach the area late Friday, moving through by late Saturday. Ahead of the shortwave, we'll see increasing moisture and decent QG lift. An upper level jet is also forecast to develop, with our area in the left exit region for much of Saturday. At the surface, a strong cold front will move through Saturday afternoon, bringing strong winds (gusting around 30 to 55mph) and much cooler temperatures. A few models are showing SBCAPE above 50J/kg on Saturday, which combined with the strong frontogenesis is causing some concern for banded snowfall and potentially even snow squalls. This and the potential for blowing snow from the strong winds could lead to hazardous travel conditions Saturday. The other thing we'll need to watch is the potential for anticyclonic turning of the winds as it comes off the Cheyenne Ridge. A slight eastward turning would increase the potential for higher snow amounts in the southern foothills, south metro, and Palmer Divide area.

The highest snow accumulations are forecast to be in the Park Range with most likely liquid totals (25th to 75th percentiles) of 0.6 to 1.6 inches. With SLRs between 10 and 15, a Winter Weather Advisory is likely once we get closer, with potential for a Winter Storm Warning. The rest of our mountain areas are currently forecast to see between 2 and 8 inches of snow with this event. For the plains, precipitation will generally be light with rain transitioning to snow behind the front. Snow accumulations are forecast to generally remain below 0.5 inches for the urban corridor and plains, with higher amounts for the Palmer and Foothills.

This system will move off to the east late Saturday, leaving colder and drier conditions for Sunday. Lows Sunday morning in the plains will be in the teens to 20s and highs will be in the 40s. Winds will remain breezy Sunday morning, putting apparent temperatures in the low teens to single digits for the eastern plains. An active pattern will continue through the middle of next week. We could see a few more chances for mountain snow next week as an upper level shortwave moves through Monday and our next bigger system approaches Wednesday.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Saturday will be fairly interesting as the day goes on. To start the morning it will be windy as the 700mb jet slowly starts moving south across the Colorado border.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - High winds are possible Thursday night through Saturday night. A High Wind Warning is currently in effect for the southeast Wyoming wind prone areas.
- Forecast uncertainty in regards to precipitation remains high for lower elevations over the weekend due to notable model variance, though mountain snow is likely.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Looking at a pleasant Thanksgiving day across southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska. Upper-level ridging will still be in place over the forecast area, leading to mild temperatures with highs roughly 5 to 10 degrees above average for late November. Mostly sunny skies will help add to the warmth, with highs in the 40s and 50s for most of the CWA. The ridge will keep precipitation chances at bay, so it'll be a good day to catch some sunshine outside before feasting on dinner. Roughly around dinner time, winds will begin to increase across southeast Wyoming as a trough digs across Canada and the northern tier of the United States. This trough will cause MSLP gradients along and west of the Laramie Range to steepen. CAG to CPR height gradients will also steepen, climbing into the 60 meter range. Height gradients this high usually indicate a higher potential for high winds around the Arlington area. Winds aloft will reach almost 60 kts with decent subsidence as well, which will aid in getting these winds down to the surface. By the time guests leave for the night, High Wind Warnings for the typical wind prone areas will be in effect. Went ahead and upgraded the High Wind Watches with this forecast package as in-house guidance also had 50 to 80 percent probabilities for high winds around Arlington, Bordeaux, and the South Laramie Range and foothills Thursday night. High winds will continue into the overnight hours Thursday, with 55 to 65 MPH gusts and localized stronger gusts up to 70 MPH. Overnight, high winds are only expected in the wind prone areas.

High winds will continue into the day Friday as the upper-level trough dips a little further south into Wyoming. While high winds will likely be persistent around Arlington and the South Laramie Range, the dip in the trough may cause more northwest winds around Bordeaux, which typically is not a favorable direction for high winds. Thus, the High Wind Warning for Bordeaux expires around 11 AM. Will have to keep an eye on some of the locations adjacent to the wind prones like the Laramie Valley and central Laramie County. There is a pretty good mountain wave signature which could send strong winds down to the surface if any waves break. For the time being, did not add any additional headlines to the wind products. High Wind Warnings for Arlington and the South Laramie Range will continue into the day Saturday. Besides the wind, increasing cloudiness is expected throughout the day ahead of another incoming progressive shortwave. High temperatures will be about the same as what they were Thursday. Unsurprisingly, high winds continue overnight Friday, but precipitation will also begin to move into the mountains as mid- level moisture increases. Snow will begin to accumulate in the mountains Friday night with winter headlines likely needed for the Sierra Madre and Snowy Ranges.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Saturday will be fairly interesting as the day goes on. To start the morning it will be windy as the 700mb jet slowly starts moving south across the Colorado border. Our wind prone areas along I-80 and I-25 will continue to have high winds to borderline highs through the morning and early afternoon we will slowly see the winds start to drop in the afternoon hours as a cold front shifts the winds from their westerly direction to a more northerly direction after the cold front passes through. While the winds will still be rather breezy into the overnight hours, the possibility of high winds significantly decreases after 21z or 2pm Saturday. A mid-level open wave will also be pushing through Saturday morning on top of our High winds. While this system doesn't appear to be totally saturated there are some plumes of moisture that will be able to produce some snowfall from the synoptic forcing alone. Albeit the only places that are going to see the snowfall in our high wind westerly pattern will be the mountain peaks for Saturday morning and early afternoon. However, the cold front will be the deciding factor for everywhere expected to pass through the forecast area by the late afternoon. A strong vorticity gradient is associated with the cold front. The vorticity gradient is fairly strong enhancing the rain and snowfall rates. Areas east of I-25 will see a faster transition from rain to snow as the cold front will reach them first as its expected to kind of pinwheel are the Laramie range as well as having less downsloping winds compared to the Lower elevations west of the I-25 corridor. The biggest problem for the lower elevations (I-25 and east) will be overcoming the dry boundary layer set in place from the downsloping winds off the breaking mountain wave. Another factor for the lower elevations will be how fast the precipitation will change over from rain to snow. With 700mb temperatures dropping down to -10c behind the cold front, the transition should be fairly quick but getting the boundary layer to reach near saturation would be needed before any precip can reach the ground. This cold airmass behind the cold front unfortunately wont stay over us long as an upper level ridge will push into the area Sunday advecting in warmer air into the region. By Monday morning the lower elevations will be in the upper 40's to lower 50's and the higher elevations will be in the mid to upper 40's. These warmer temperatures are expected to continue through mid-week and likely melting any snow that accumulated that is not on the mountain top.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Though impacts look greatest for the Park Range, concerns for impactful snowfall over the Flat Tops and central Colorado mountains are manifesting as well. The former is looking more and more favorable to hit advisory-level snow.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mild and dry conditions expected through Thanksgiving.
- Snow is expected late Friday and through Saturday, primarily over the Park Range. The Flat Tops and central Colorado mountains are also expected to be impacted.
- An unsettled pattern looks to continue into next week with potential for more mountain snow, but details remain uncertain.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: MILD AND DRY CONDITIONS THROUGH THANKSGIVING:

A ridge is situated overhead with little more than high clouds passing through the region. Thanksgiving Day will be characterized by near-normal moisture, and as a result, region- wide weather will be calm. Temperatures will be 5 to 10 degrees above normal Thanksgiving Day as well.
SNOWY AFTER THANKSGIVING INTO THE WEEKEND:

On Friday, moisture originating from a PacNW AR will descend into the Intermountain West through northwesterly flow. The bulk of that moisture will reside to our north, but ensembles are indicating that the northeastern corner of our CWA will get clipped by PWAT's up to 200% of normal. This sparks our next round of impactful weather. The onset of measurable precipitation is expected to occur late afternoon to early evening Friday with most precipitation driven by orographics and anchored to the high terrain. Though moisture is expected to begin declining around sunrise Saturday, models are showing the strongest snow rates during this period. This is mostly driven by a transient shortwave embedded in the northwesterly flow, and as such, we should see an uptick in snow rates both over the mountains and into some higher elevation valleys and basins in north-central Colorado through the late morning and into the afternoon.

As seen in the latest forecast, snow totals are on the rise. With the upward trend of snow totals for the weekend storm, the low end snow scenario looks safely at or above advisory level (6+ inches) for the Park Range. The NBM backs this up with a greater than 80% probability of 6 or more inches of snow above 9000 feet, which would include Rabbit Ears Pass. Below this elevation though, probability of advisory-level snow accumulations sharply drop off. For those areas in the Park Range expected to receive the bulk of snowfall, the question is what the high end scenario could be. Per the NBM, probabilities of accumulations exceeding a foot stand at over 70%. In spite of the high chances, we are cautious to call for 12+ inches over the Park Range just yet due to lacking consistency between forecasts. Though guidance is trending towards higher accumulations, we will wait to see where model guidance settles before speculating on amounts.

Though impacts look greatest for the Park Range, concerns for impactful snowfall over the Flat Tops and central Colorado mountains are manifesting as well. The former is looking more and more favorable to hit advisory-level snow. Confidence has decreased on exact values over the past twelve hours, but this is due to 75th percentile snow forecasts jumping up. So, just like the Park Range, forecasts are trending upwards for snow totals in the Flat Tops. As for the latter, confidence in accumulations has notably increased according to the NBM, though it is still anticipated to see the least precipitation among the areas of interest. Given the northerly track of the storm, elevations at pass level and below are likely to struggle to reach 6 inches. However, with roads likely to be busier with post-holiday travel, even lighter accumulations will pose heightened travel risks. As such, be mindful of difficult driving conditions through the mountains should you find yourself on the roads Saturday.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Monday through Thursday...broad zonal westerly flow is forecast to fill in behind the departing wave, with periods of light snow for the Central Mountains, and warming conditions across the Plains, back into the 50s.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Quiet weather today and Friday, with increasing winds on Friday along with warming temperatures.
- A strong shortwave trough will pass across the region Saturday, with light high elevation snow, and very strong winds across the Plains.
- Some uncertainty exists into mid next week with the next upper storm system.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...satellite imagery shows increasing mid and high level cloud cover spreading across the state early this morning. This is associated with a weak passing wave. Overall, temperatures are in the 20s and 30s, with most areas in the teens and 20s by daybreak. There could be some patchy fog across the lower Arkansas River Valley near the Kansas border through morning.

Today and tonight...upper level high pressure will settle across southern California, with broad northwesterly flow across Colorado. Mid and high level cloud cover will track east across the region through this afternoon with weak energy dropping southeast in the flow aloft, clearing overnight. No precipitation is forecast. Today's high temperatures will top out in the 50s across the lower elevations. Lows tonight will fall into the 20s and 30s across the Plains, with the warmest reading along the Eastern Mountain lee slopes.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Models in much better agreement tonight through the extended period. A quick moving trough will bring a few mountain snow showers to the Central Mountains Saturday, along with strong winds for the Plains.

Friday...increasing northwesterly flow aloft continues on Friday through the overnight hours. Enhanced mixing will lead to warming conditions, with most areas on the Plains well into the 60s, with a few areas near 70 degrees. The San Luis Valley will warm into the 50s. Winds will also be on the increase, especially in gap wind prone areas along the I-25 corridor. Gusts 30 to 35 mph may be possible. Humidity values look to remain elevated above 20 percent. While dry conditions are forecast on Friday, a couple of light snow showers may move into the Central Mountains late in the day. During the overnight hours, a shortwave trough is forecast to strength across Utah, forcing flow more westerly across southern Colorado. Showers look to increase in coverage from the La Garita Range, north into the Central Mountains. Little if any snow accumulations are forecast overnight. Winds will also remain elevated across the higher terrain and along the lee slopes of the Eastern Mountains. Overnight lows will fall into the 20s for the San Luis Valley, with the Plains ranging from the 40s west of I-25, to 30s east.

Saturday and Sunday...the upper trough is forecast to track across southern Colorado Saturday, clearing into the Central Plains by Sunday morning. Snow showers will be on the increase across the higher terrain, with the main focus across the Central Mountains. Snow accumulations look minor, with 1 to 3 inches possible north of Cottonwood Pass through Saturday evening.

Winds will be the main concern across the Plains on Saturday. A very strong cold front will drop south by mid to late morning, shifting winds northerly into the afternoon. Wind gusts 40 to 50 mph will be possible, with higher gusts near the Kansas border. DESI 58 mph probs are 30-50 percent for portions of the Plains, and we will continue to monitor trends for possible high wind highlights. Travel could be difficult on west-east highways due to strong cross winds.

Another concern may be spotty rain and snow showers moving off the higher terrain and into the Palmer Divide Saturday evening. Temperatures will be falling, from the 50s to lower 60s earlier in the day to 30s and 40s during the evening. Rain and snow driven by strong winds may produce brief window for hazardous travel Saturday evening north of Woodmen Road to Monument Hill. We will continue to monitor this possibility.

Snow winds down across the higher terrain overnight, ending by Sunday morning. Across the Plains, a few showers may be possible behind the front, mostly along the southern I-25 corridor. Little if any impacts are expected outside of possibly the Palmer Divide. All precipitation should be done by Sunday morning. Winds will remain brisk across the Plains on Sunday, with highs on the Plains reaching the upper 30s to 40s.

Monday through Thursday...broad zonal westerly flow is forecast to fill in behind the departing wave, with periods of light snow for the Central Mountains, and warming conditions across the Plains, back into the 50s. The next storm system is possible Wednesday into Thursday, but trends and differences in model guidance lead to uncertainty mid week.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Saturday's maxes should return to near normal for this time of year, but rebuilding high pressure will bring increasingly mild temperatures for the early part of the upcoming week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions will persist for Thanksgiving Day with temperatures near seasonal normals. Temperatures will be increasingly mild for Friday, with maxes around 5-10F above seasonal normals.
- A weak storm system will move across northern Utah late Friday into Saturday, bringing generally light valley rain and mountain snow to northern Utah and southwest Wyoming.
- Dry conditions will return for the weekend with increasingly mild temperatures, with an active pattern expected to return by the middle of the upcoming week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: High pressure is centered off the southern California coast his morning, bringing a dry northwest flow to Utah and southwest Wyoming. Seeing some high clouds from a Pacific Northwest storm system passing well to the north of the area, but otherwise conditions are tranquil with highs expected to be near seasonal normals once again.

The ridge is expected to flatten during the day across the area tomorrow as a strong Pacific Northwest storm system approaches, bringing an increasing westerly flow, allowing for better mixing in currently inverted valleys and warmer temperatures, with maxes running 5-10F above seasonal normals. This trough is eventually expected to cross northern Utah and southwest Wyoming Friday night into Saturday morning, bringing light valley rain/mountain snow to northern portions of the area, primarily north of I-80. Overall, guidance is trending northward with the track of this system, thus limiting the southern extent of this precipitation.

Saturday's maxes should return to near normal for this time of year, but rebuilding high pressure will bring increasingly mild temperatures for the early part of the upcoming week. Guidance continues to indicate the potential of a more significant storm system to impact the area for the middle to latter part of the upcoming week, but a large subset of the guidance is indicating this might be an event primarily for southern Utah. Still, confidence in any solution remains low this far out.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: You can trigger a slab avalanche near and above treeline on the north half of the compass on slopes steeper than about 30 degrees. These avalanches can be large enough to bury or injury you. Give drifted slopes a wide berth; you might trigger them from above, next to, or below.
Seek out wind-sheltered areas and slopes below treeline for safer travel options.

2753.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: You can still trigger a dangerous avalanche where you encounter older wind-drifted slabs below ridgelines, especially on northwest through north to east-facing slopes at upper elevations. You might trigger them from thin spots above, adjacent to, or below the drifted features. Choose wind-sheltered terrain to avoid the problem.

2754.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe from avalanches due to thin and discontinuous snow cover. You can trigger a small avalanche in wind-drifted snow above treeline. Look for these drifts below ridges and around rocky outcrops on slopes facing west through north to east.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe to travel on as there is very little snow. In the alpine, steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetops.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

1736.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Elevations above 7,000 feet have 1-2 feet of snow on the ground. You may encounter pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north- and east-facing terrain. If the snow feels stiff or slabby underfoot, then find a different aspect away from wind-drifted snow. The biggest hazard remains thin snow cover and hitting rocks, logs, and stumps. Even a small slide through thin coverage could end a season before it even starts.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: Above 7,000 feet, a layered snowpack is beginning to build for the season. Good, albeit thin, skiing and riding conditions have been reported at upper elevations. Elevations below 7,000 feet remain thin and bony. Before November 13th, most slopes were bare. Winter trailhead access remains a challenge as there is not quite enough snow to launch sleds. Most forest roads become impassable by vehicle above 6,500 feet. As folks start poking around the mountains, remember that avalanches can occur with just a few feet of snow on the ground. There may be some lingering pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north and east-facing terrain features, particularly just below ridgelines.

Beginning Thanksgiving Day, a large storm system will impact the Pacific and Interior Northwest. Strong winds, mountain snow, and fluctuating rain/snow levels will be in the cards for several days. Pay attention to changing weather and snow conditions heading into the weekend. Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

Fresh wind slabs will come back onto the menu with more snow and wind later this week. Pay attention to gullies that can become crossloaded and may also act as a terrain trap. Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices. Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
Turn On Your Snow and Avalanche Brain

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).

• Help us paint a picture of what's going on in the mountains. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps forecasters and the public alike.
